transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A major community garden project in Detroit, Michigan, is transforming abandoned city lots into productive green spaces that provide fresh produce to local residents. The initiative, launched three years ago by a non-profit organization called Urban Harvest, has already converted more than 50 vacant properties into thriving gardens where neighbors grow vegetables, fruits, and herbs. According to project organizers, the gardens not only address food insecurity in underserved neighborhoods but also create gathering spaces that strengthen community bonds. Local volunteers, including many high school students, help maintain the gardens and distribute the harvest to families in need. The organization reports that last year alone, they donated over 20,000 pounds of fresh produce to local food banks. City officials have praised the project and recently announced plans to allocate additional funding to expand the program to other parts of the city. Similar urban gardening initiatives have been launched in several other Rust Belt cities, inspired by Detroit's success.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: The world's largest passenger aircraft, the Airbus A380, may be making a comeback as airlines reconsider their fleet strategies in response to changing travel patterns. During the pandemic, many airlines grounded their A380s, with some carriers announcing permanent retirement of the double-decker planes. However, as international travel demand surges to pre-pandemic levels, several major airlines are now bringing their A380s back into service. Aviation analysts say the aircraft's high capacity makes it particularly efficient for busy long-haul routes where airport slots are limited. Emirates, the largest operator of the A380, has already returned more than 80 of its superjumbos to service and reports strong passenger demand for the spacious aircraft. Other airlines including Lufthansa and Qantas have also reversed earlier decisions to retire their A380 fleets. Airbus, which ceased production of the A380 in 2021, says it will continue providing maintenance support for existing aircraft for decades to come.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A new study from Cambridge University suggests that learning a musical instrument during childhood can have significant long-term benefits for brain development, particularly in areas related to hearing and memory. The research followed 700 young adults, comparing those who had received at least two years of formal music training before the age of 12 with those who had no musical training. Participants were given a series of cognitive tests while their brain activity was monitored using MRI scans. The results showed that individuals with early musical training performed 20 percent better on memory tasks and were more adept at processing speech in noisy environments compared to the control group. Interestingly, the benefits were observed even in participants who had stopped playing their instrument years earlier. Lead researcher Dr. Sarah Mitchell emphasized that the study does not prove that music makes people smarter overall, but rather that it strengthens specific neural pathways that can be useful in everyday situations.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Woman (Lisa): Hey, Mark, are you okay? You look really stressed out.
Man (Mark): Oh hi, Lisa. Yeah, I'm just feeling overwhelmed. I have three papers due next week, and I haven't even started two of them. Plus I have to work 20 hours at the campus café this week.
Woman: That sounds really tough. Have you talked to your professors about extensions? Sometimes they're pretty understanding if you explain your situation.
Man: I thought about that, but I don't want to seem like I'm not managing my time well. I'm also worried that if I get behind, I'll never catch up.

Woman: Well, speaking from experience, most professors would rather you ask for an extension than turn in a rushed, low-quality paper. Last semester I had a family emergency, and all three of my professors gave me extra time without any penalty.
Man: Really? Which professors are most flexible? The one I'm most worried about is Professor Davis for economics. I heard he's really strict about deadlines.

Woman: Actually, Professor Davis gave me an extension once! I was really surprised too. He just asked me to send him an email explaining the circumstances. As long as you don't make a habit of it, he's pretty reasonable.
Man: That's a relief. Do you have any tips for managing the workload besides asking for extensions? I'm really struggling with time management lately.

Woman: Have you tried using a planner? Not just writing down due dates, but actually scheduling specific times to work on each paper? I also find that breaking big projects into smaller tasks makes them feel less intimidating. Instead of "write research paper," I'll write things like "find five sources," "write outline," "draft introduction," and so on.
Man: That actually makes a lot of sense. I usually just look at the whole assignment and panic. Do you use a paper planner or an app?

Woman: I use both, actually. I have a wall calendar above my desk for big deadlines, and I use a phone app for daily tasks. But honestly, even just a simple notebook works if you're consistent with it. The key is to write everything down instead of trying to remember it all.

Man: I think I'll give that a try. I have a planner somewhere that I haven't opened since the first week of classes. Also, do you know if the library has any study rooms available? I can never get any work done in my dorm—my roommate is always playing video games.

Woman: The library's study rooms get booked up pretty quickly, but there are usually quiet carrels available on the fourth floor. Those work really well for me when I need to focus. Also, have you checked out the new student success center? They have drop-in tutoring and even time management workshops.
Man: No, I didn't know about that. Where is it again?

Woman: It's in the basement of the Student Union building. I went to a time management workshop there last month, and it was really helpful. They talked about identifying your peak productivity hours—like, I'm a morning person, so I try to do my hardest work before noon.

Man: That's interesting. I'm definitely a night owl, so maybe I should schedule my study time in the evenings instead of forcing myself to get up early. I always feel guilty when I sleep in, but maybe that's just when my brain works best.

Woman: Exactly! Don't try to force someone else's schedule. Figure out what works for you. And hey, don't forget to take breaks too. I use the Pomodoro Technique—25 minutes of focused work, then a 5-minute break. It really helps prevent burnout.
Man: Thanks so much, Lisa. I feel better already just having a plan. I'm going to email my professors tonight and then map out my week in my planner tomorrow.
Woman: You've got this! And if you need someone to proofread your papers or bring you coffee during a study session, just let me know.
Man: That's really kind of you. I'll definitely take you up on that coffee offer.

Woman: Oh, absolutely worth every penny! The admission is 12 pounds for adults, but students get in for half price, and I think it's free on Thursday evenings. I went on Sunday with my sister, and we spent almost three hours there.
Man: That sounds like quite a long time. What makes it so special? I usually go through art exhibits pretty quickly—I'm not much of an art expert.

Woman: Neither am I, honestly, but this one is different. Each photograph has a little audio story you can listen to by scanning a QR code with your phone. The photographers talk about what inspired them and the stories behind the shots. It makes the whole experience much more immersive.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: Public libraries have undergone a remarkable transformation over the past two decades, evolving from quiet buildings filled primarily with books into dynamic community hubs that offer an incredible range of services and resources. While books remain central to their mission, modern libraries now lend everything from power tools and kitchen equipment to musical instruments and camping gear. Many offer free access to 3D printers, recording studios, and digital media labs, giving community members access to technology they might not be able to afford on their own.

Perhaps most importantly, libraries have become critical centers for digital inclusion. According to the American Library Association, nearly 100 percent of public libraries in the United States offer free Wi-Fi and public computers, and millions of people rely on these services for job searching, online learning, and accessing government services. During the pandemic, many libraries expanded their Wi-Fi signals into parking lots so that students without home internet could still attend online classes.

Libraries also play an increasingly important role in supporting early literacy and lifelong learning. Children's story hours, summer reading programs, and homework help sessions are staples at most branches, but many now offer coding classes for kids, citizenship preparation courses for immigrants, and even financial literacy workshops for adults. The concept of the library as a "third place"—not home, not work, but a welcoming space where community members can gather and connect—has become more important than ever. Despite predictions that the internet would make libraries obsolete, usage has remained strong, demonstrating that these institutions fulfill a vital need in communities that goes far beyond lending books.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Have you ever wondered why certain songs get stuck in your head, playing on repeat for hours or even days? These involuntary musical experiences, commonly known as earworms, are actually a fascinating cognitive phenomenon that researchers are only beginning to understand fully.

First, let's consider how common earworms are. Studies suggest that over 90 percent of people experience them at least once a week, with some people having them daily. They typically last between 15 and 30 seconds, though some can persist much longer. Certain types of music are more likely to become earworms than others. Researchers have found that songs with simple, repetitive melodies and unusual rhythms or intervals tend to be stickier. Interestingly, songs with lyrics are more likely to get stuck than instrumental pieces, and faster songs are more common as earworms than slower ones.

But why do our brains do this? Cognitive scientists have proposed several theories. One leading theory suggests that earworms happen when our brains get stuck in a loop trying to complete a musical phrase. This explains why songs with a clear, repetitive structure are more likely to become stuck. Another theory connects earworms to memory and attention—they often occur when we're doing tasks that don't require our full attention, like walking, cleaning, or showering.

Emotional factors also play a significant role. Songs that trigger strong emotional responses, whether positive or negative, are more likely to become earworms. Music we hear during important life events tends to come back to us more often as well. There's even a connection between personality and earworm susceptibility—people who score higher on measures of neuroticism tend to experience earworms more frequently and find them more distressing.

So what can you do if you have a particularly stubborn earworm? Researchers have tested several strategies. One surprisingly effective method is to engage with the song fully—listen to it all the way through instead of trying to push it away, which gives your brain the closure it needs. Another technique is to give your brain something else to focus on, particularly a verbal task like solving an anagram or reading a complex article. Chewing gum has also been shown in some studies to help, possibly because it occupies the same brain systems involved in verbal rehearsal. And contrary to popular belief, trying to suppress the song actively often makes it worse—a phenomenon psychologists call the rebound effect.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The concept of vertical farming—growing crops in vertically stacked layers, often in controlled indoor environments—has been gaining attention as a potential solution to feeding our growing global population while reducing agriculture's environmental impact. Proponents argue that vertical farms could revolutionize food production, but it's important to consider both the advantages and challenges of this technology.

On the positive side, vertical farming offers several impressive benefits. First and foremost, it uses dramatically less water than traditional agriculture—up to 95 percent less, according to some estimates, because water is recirculated within the system. Vertical farms can also produce crops year-round without being affected by weather, droughts, or seasonal changes. Since most are located in or near urban areas, transportation distances are drastically reduced, meaning less fuel consumption and fresher produce reaching consumers. Additionally, because crops are grown in controlled environments, there's no need for pesticides or herbicides, and crops can be grown without soil using hydroponic or aeroponic systems. Vertical farms also use space extremely efficiently; one acre of vertical growing space can produce the equivalent of 10 to 20 acres of traditional farmland.

However, vertical farming faces significant challenges that have prevented widespread adoption so far. The biggest barrier is cost—setting up and operating a vertical farm is extremely expensive due to the need for specialized lighting, climate control systems, and ongoing energy costs. Even with LED lighting improvements, the electricity required to power indoor farms remains substantial, leading to concerns about the carbon footprint unless renewable energy is used. Labor costs can also be high, as vertical farming requires workers with specialized technical skills.

Another challenge is that not all crops are suitable for vertical farming. Leafy greens like lettuce, spinach, and herbs grow well in these systems and are currently the most common crops produced commercially. However, staple crops like wheat, corn, and rice—which provide the majority of calories globally—require too much space and energy to grow vertically to be economically viable with current technology. Some fruits and vegetables, like tomatoes and peppers, have been grown successfully, but they present their own challenges.

Despite these hurdles, the vertical farming industry continues to grow and evolve. Technological advances are bringing down costs, and many experts believe that as the technology improves, vertical farms will become an increasingly important part of our food system, working alongside traditional agriculture rather than replacing it entirely.
